## Summary
Given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return their intersection as a list of the unique values present in both. The input is two arrays (possibly with duplicates); the output contains each common element exactly once, order unspecified.

## Why it matters
Using a hash set for membership testing is the standard way to turn an O(n*m) nested-loop comparison into linear time, and "build a set, then filter" is one of the most reused patterns in data-processing code (deduplication, joins, allow-lists).

## Idea
- Insert every element of `nums1` into a hash set, giving O(1) average membership checks.
- Iterate over `nums2`; if an element is in the set, it is a common value, so add it to the result.
- Immediately delete that key from the set after emitting it, which guarantees each common value is reported only once even if `nums2` repeats it.
- This single-pass-per-array approach avoids sorting and avoids quadratic comparison.

## Complexity
Time O(n + m), space O(n) — one set holds the distinct elements of `nums1`, and each array is scanned once.

## Pitfalls
- Without removing the matched key (or using a separate "seen" set), repeated values in `nums2` would produce duplicate output.
- Using `map[int]bool` works but `map[int]struct{}` better signals a set and uses no value storage.
- The result order is not guaranteed and should not be relied upon.
- A `nil` result slice is returned when there is no intersection, which is fine in Go but worth noting for callers expecting an empty (non-nil) slice.

## Summary
Implement the fan-out / fan-in concurrency pattern: a producer emits a stream of values, multiple worker goroutines/threads process them in parallel (fan-out), and their results are merged back into a single output stream (fan-in). The Go version multiplexes several source channels into one; the Rust version distributes one producer's items across `worker_count` workers and collects the squared results.

## Why it matters
Fan-out / fan-in is the backbone of concurrent pipelines: it parallelizes CPU- or IO-bound stages while keeping a single ordered drain point. The correct shutdown choreography (closing channels exactly once, after all senders finish) is the part engineers most often get wrong in production worker pools.

## Idea
- Fan-out: start N independent consumers that all read from the same source. In Go each source channel gets its own goroutine; in Rust the single `Receiver` is shared behind an `Arc<Mutex<>>` so workers compete for items.
- Fan-in: every worker writes into one shared output channel.
- The critical invariant is closing the output exactly once, only after all producers/workers are done. Go uses a `sync.WaitGroup`: each merge goroutine calls `Done`, and a separate goroutine does `wg.Wait()` then `close(out)`.
- In Rust, each worker holds a clone of the result `Sender`; once the producer drops its sender the source disconnects, workers see `Disconnected` and exit, dropping their senders. After the original `work_tx` is also dropped, the collector's `for val in work_rx` loop ends naturally.
- Because the result channel is unbounded, the main thread can safely join workers before draining it.

## Complexity
Time O(items) total work spread across the worker pool; space O(workers + channel buffer). Concretely: 1 producer goroutine/thread, N worker goroutines/threads, and 1 closer goroutine (Go), communicating over channels rather than shared memory.

## Pitfalls
- Closing the output channel from a worker, or closing it more than once, panics ("send on closed channel" / double close); close only after `wg.Wait()` from a single owner.
- Forgetting to drop/clone senders correctly leaves the fan-in loop blocked forever (deadlock) because the receiver never sees disconnection.
- In the Rust shared-receiver design, holding the mutex lock across the whole processing step serializes the workers; lock only long enough to pull an item.
- Busy-spinning with `try_recv` + sleep burns CPU; a blocking `recv` (or a bounded channel) is usually preferable, though it complicates clean shutdown.

## Задача
Есть несколько независимых источников данных, каждый асинхронно выдаёт числа в свой канал. Нужно объединить их в один поток (паттерн **fan-out / fan-in**).

## Что реализовать
- `gen(data []int, delay time.Duration) <-chan int` — генератор: возвращает канал, в который по одному (с задержкой `delay`) шлёт элементы `data`, затем закрывает канал.
- `merge(chans ...<-chan int) <-chan int` — fan-in: конкурентно читает из всех входных каналов и сливает значения в один выходной; закрывает его, когда все источники исчерпаны.

## Требования
- `merge` не теряет значения и не зависает.
- Выходной канал закрывается ровно один раз, после завершения всех источников (через `sync.WaitGroup` + отдельная горутина-закрыватель).
- Канал нельзя закрывать из нескольких горутин.
- Аккуратно передавай канал в горутину (без захвата переменной цикла).

## Пример
3 источника `[1,2,3]`, `[4,5,6]`, `[7,8,9]` → на выходе все 9 чисел в произвольном порядке.

## Summary
Run a long-running operation but give up if it exceeds a deadline. The input is a `context.Context` carrying a timeout; the output is the operation's result and `nil`, or a zero value and a timeout error if the deadline fires first. Here `longOperation` sleeps a random 0-4 seconds and the context allows 2 seconds.

## Why it matters
Bounding work with a deadline is fundamental for resilient servers: every outbound RPC, DB query, or HTTP call should be cancellable so a slow dependency cannot pin a goroutine forever. `context.WithTimeout` is the idiomatic Go way to propagate deadlines through a call tree.

## Idea
- Create a deadline-bearing context with `context.WithTimeout(parent, d)` and always `defer cancel()` to release its resources.
- Launch the blocking work in a separate goroutine that sends its result on a buffered channel (capacity 1) so the goroutine never leaks if the receiver has already moved on.
- `select` over two cases: `<-ctx.Done()` (deadline/cancel) versus `<-ch` (result). Whichever is ready first wins.
- The buffer matters: if the timeout case fires, the worker can still send into the buffered channel and exit cleanly instead of blocking forever.

## Complexity
O(1) coordination overhead plus the cost of the operation itself; O(1) extra space (one goroutine and a 1-slot channel).

## Pitfalls
- Using an unbuffered result channel leaks the goroutine on timeout, because no one will ever receive its send.
- `context.Context(...)` is not a constructor; the timed context comes from `context.WithTimeout`.
- Forgetting `defer cancel()` leaks the timer until the parent context is canceled.
- On error you must actually print/propagate the error value, not a bare label.

## Задача
Запустить долгую операцию и прервать **ожидание** по таймауту через `context`. Сама операция отменяться не умеет — нужно перестать её ждать.

## Что реализовать
- `callWithTimeout(ctx context.Context) (int, error)` — запускает `longOperation()` в горутине и возвращает её результат; если `ctx` отменён (истёк таймаут) раньше, чем пришёл результат — возвращает `(0, error)`.

## Требования
- Используй `select` по `ctx.Done()` и каналу результата.
- Канал результата должен быть **буферизованным** (`cap 1`), иначе после таймаута горутина навсегда зависнет на отправке → утечка горутины.
- Не блокироваться дольше таймаута.

## Пример
`longOperation` спит 0..5с, таймаут 2с → результат либо `Result: 42`, либо `Error: timeout exceeded`.

## Summary
Reproduce Go's `context.WithTimeout` and cancellation in Rust, which has no built-in context type. Provide a `with_timeout` helper that runs a closure on a worker thread and returns `Ok(value)` if it finishes within a `Duration`, otherwise a timeout error; and a `cancellable_work` loop that stops early when a cancel signal arrives on a channel.

## Why it matters
Rust's standard library models cancellation and deadlines with `mpsc` channels rather than a context object. Knowing `recv_timeout` and `try_recv` lets you bound blocking work and implement cooperative cancellation without pulling in an async runtime.

## Idea
- For timeout: spawn the closure on a thread that sends its result through an `mpsc` channel, then block on `rx.recv_timeout(timeout)`. A `Timeout` error means the deadline elapsed; `Disconnected` means the worker panicked/dropped the sender.
- For cancellation: the worker loops and on each iteration calls `cancel_rx.try_recv()`; if it gets `Ok(())` (signal sent) or `Disconnected` (sender dropped) it returns early, while `Empty` means keep going. This is cooperative cancellation — the work itself must poll.
- The result channel lets the caller distinguish "completed with a value" from "cancelled before finishing" via `try_recv`.

## Complexity
O(work) time bounded by the timeout; O(1) extra space per call (one worker thread plus a single-message channel). Cancellation polling adds O(1) per loop iteration.

## Pitfalls
- `recv_timeout` blocks the calling thread; the spawned worker keeps running even after a timeout (Rust threads are not forcibly killable), so this is a soft timeout for the caller, not true preemption.
- Treat `Disconnected` explicitly — a panicked worker drops the sender and you must not interpret that as success.
- Cancellation is cooperative: if the loop body is a single long blocking call, the cancel signal will not be observed until the next `try_recv`.
- Reading the result with `try_recv` right after `join` is fine here, but in general prefer `recv` if you must wait for the value.

## Summary
Build a fixed-size worker pool that consumes integers from an input channel, processes each one (multiply by 10 after a random delay), and emits results on an output channel — all governed by a `context.Context` so the whole pipeline stops on timeout or cancellation. The input is a stream of jobs plus a context with a 3-second deadline; the output is the processed values.

## Why it matters
Worker pools are the canonical way to cap concurrency in Go: instead of spawning one goroutine per job you reuse N workers, bounding resource usage. Combining the pool with a context gives clean, propagating cancellation across the producer, workers, and consumer — the standard fan-out/fan-in pattern in production services.

## Idea
- A producer goroutine feeds `in` and closes it when done, using `select` on `ctx.Done()` so it stops feeding if the deadline hits.
- Start `workers` goroutines, each tracked by a `sync.WaitGroup`. Each worker loops over a `select`: on `ctx.Done()` it returns; on a value from `in` it processes and pushes to `out`. Receiving `ok == false` means `in` closed, so the worker returns.
- Sends to `out` are themselves wrapped in a `select` with `ctx.Done()` so a worker never blocks forever if the consumer is gone.
- A single coordinating goroutine calls `wg.Wait()` and then closes `out` exactly once, signalling the consumer's `range` loop to finish. `out` must be a send-only (`chan<-`) channel inside the pool and be closed in only one place.

## Complexity
O(N/W) wall-clock time for N jobs across W workers plus per-job processing cost; O(W) goroutines and O(1) channel buffers — constant extra space beyond the pool.

## Pitfalls
- Closing `out` from more than one place (e.g. both the pool and `main`) causes a "close of closed channel" panic; close it exactly once after `wg.Wait()`.
- A worker that receives but never sends to `out` silently drops results; make sure every consumed job produces an output (or is intentionally skipped on cancel).
- Direction-typed channels matter: declaring `out` as `<-chan int` (receive-only) makes sending to it a compile error.
- If `wg.Wait()` runs in the same goroutine that should also feed work, you deadlock — keep the close-after-wait in its own goroutine relative to the consumer.

## Задача
Пул из N воркеров обрабатывает поток заданий из входного канала и шлёт результаты в выходной. Всё должно корректно завершаться по закрытию входа и уважать отмену через `context`.

## Что реализовать
- `processWithCtx(ctx context.Context, v int) (int, bool)` — обрабатывает значение (`process(v)`), но прерывается по `ctx`; второй возврат `false`, если отменено.
- `workerPool(ctx context.Context, in <-chan int, out chan<- int, workers int)` — запускает `workers` горутин; каждая читает из `in`, обрабатывает через `processWithCtx`, шлёт в `out`; завершается при закрытии `in` **или** отмене `ctx`. Возвращает управление после завершения всех воркеров.

## Требования
- Отправка в `out` тоже под `select` с `ctx.Done()` — иначе воркер зависнет, если получатель ушёл.
- Никаких гонок и двойного `close`. `out` закрывает вызывающая сторона (в `main`) после `workerPool`.
- Закрытие `in` штатно останавливает воркеров (`v, ok := <-in; if !ok { return }`).

## Пример
Вход `1..20`, 4 воркера, таймаут 3с → в `out` приходят числа, умноженные на 10.

# Задание 4: asyncio — базовые паттерны

import asyncio
from typing import Any

# --- Базовая корутина ---

async def fetch_data(url: str, delay: float) -> str:
    print(f"fetching {url}...")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f"data from {url}"

# --- Параллельный запуск через gather ---

async def fetch_all(urls: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    tasks = [fetch_data(url, delay=0.1 * i) for i, url in enumerate(urls)]
    results = await asyncio.gather(* tasks)
    return results

# --- asyncio.create_task ---

async def process_with_tasks():
    task1 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data("api/users", 0.2))
    task2 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data("api/orders", 0.2))

    # Задачи уже запущены параллельно, ждём обе
    result1 = await task1
    result2 = await task2

    return result1, result2

# --- Таймаут ---

async def fetch_with_timeout(url: str, timeout: float) -> str | None:
    try:
        result = await asyncio.wait_for(fetch_data(url, 5.0), timeout=timeout)
        return result
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        print(f"timeout fetching {url}")
        return None

# --- Семафор — ограничение параллелизма ---

async def limited_fetch(sem: asyncio.Semaphore, url: str, delay: float) -> str:
    async with sem:
        return await fetch_data(url, delay)

async def fetch_with_concurrency(urls: list[str], max_concurrent: int) -> list[str]:
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(max_concurrent)
    tasks = [limited_fetch(sem, url, 0.1) for url in urls]
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

# --- Producer-Consumer через asyncio.Queue ---

async def producer(queue: asyncio.Queue, items: list[str]):
    for item in items:
        await queue.put(item)
        print(f"produced: {item}")
    await queue.put(None) # сигнал остановки

async def consumer(queue: asyncio.Queue, name: str):
    while True:
        item = await queue.get()
        if item is None:
            await queue.put(None)  # пробросить для других consumers
            break
        print(f"[{name}] consumed: {item}")
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        queue.task_done()

async def producer_consumer_demo():
    queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2)

    prod = asyncio.create_task(producer(queue, ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]))
    cons1 = asyncio.create_task(consumer(queue, "worker-1"))
    cons2 = asyncio.create_task(consumer(queue, "worker-2"))

    await prod
    await cons1
    await cons2

# --- Запуск ---

async def main():
    # gather
    urls = ["api/a", "api/b", "api/c"]
    results = await fetch_all(urls)
    print(f"gathered: {results}\n")

    # create_task
    r1, r2 = await process_with_tasks()
    print(f"tasks: {r1}, {r2}\n")

    # timeout
    result = await fetch_with_timeout("api/slow", 0.2)
    print(f"timeout result: {result}\n")

    # semaphore
    urls = [f"api/{i}" for i in range(6)]
    results = await fetch_with_concurrency(urls, max_concurrent=2)
    print(f"limited: {len(results)} results\n")

    # producer-consumer
    await producer_consumer_demo()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

## Summary
Demonstrate the core asyncio building blocks: an `async def` coroutine, concurrent execution with `asyncio.gather`, eager scheduling with `asyncio.create_task`, deadlines via `asyncio.wait_for`, concurrency limiting with `asyncio.Semaphore`, and a producer/consumer pipeline over `asyncio.Queue`. The "input" is a set of simulated URLs and delays; the output is the gathered results and queue-consumed items.

## Why it matters
Async I/O is how Python services handle thousands of concurrent network calls on a single thread without blocking. These primitives — gather, tasks, timeouts, semaphores, queues — are the everyday vocabulary of any aiohttp/FastAPI/async-database codebase.

## Idea
- `await` on a coroutine runs it to completion; `asyncio.gather(*coros)` schedules many coroutines concurrently on one event loop and returns their results in order.
- `asyncio.create_task` immediately schedules a coroutine so it starts running before you await it, enabling overlap between two independent operations.
- `asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout)` cancels the coroutine and raises `asyncio.TimeoutError` if it does not finish in time.
- `asyncio.Semaphore(n)` used as `async with sem` caps how many coroutines run the protected section at once.
- The producer/consumer demo uses a bounded `asyncio.Queue`; the producer enqueues a sentinel `None` to signal completion, and each consumer re-enqueues the sentinel before breaking so sibling consumers also terminate.

## Complexity
Wall-clock time is dominated by the longest concurrent batch rather than the sum of delays; memory is O(number of pending tasks + queue size). The semaphore section serializes to at most `max_concurrent` simultaneous coroutines.

## Pitfalls
- Calling `await` on coroutines one-by-one instead of `gather`/`create_task` serializes them and loses the concurrency benefit.
- A single sentinel with multiple consumers requires re-injecting `None` after consuming it, or remaining consumers hang on `queue.get()` forever.
- `wait_for` raises `TimeoutError`, not a returned `None` — you must catch it; and the underlying coroutine is cancelled, so guard any cleanup.
- Blocking (synchronous) calls inside a coroutine freeze the entire event loop; only `await`-able operations yield control.

## Summary
Build a thread-based worker pool that pulls tasks from a queue and runs them concurrently. The input is a stream of submitted callables with arguments; the required output is the collected results (or captured exceptions) for each task plus a count of processed tasks. The pool must support graceful shutdown that drains all pending work.

## Why it matters
Worker pools are the standard way to bound concurrency for I/O-bound work in Python where the GIL makes raw threads useful for waiting (network, disk) rather than CPU. The same producer/consumer + bounded queue pattern appears in job runners, crawlers, and request pipelines.

## Idea
- A fixed set of daemon threads each loop, calling `tasks.get(timeout=...)` and continuing on `queue.Empty` so they can re-check a shutdown `threading.Event`.
- Each task is a `(func, args, kwargs)` tuple; the worker runs it inside a try/except and pushes `(worker_id, result, error)` onto a results queue, so a failing task never kills the thread.
- `task_done()` in a `finally` keeps the queue's unfinished-task count accurate, letting `tasks.join()` block until every submitted item is processed.
- `shutdown(wait=True)` first joins the task queue (drain), then sets the event and joins the threads, guaranteeing no work is lost.
- An `AtomicCounter` guarded by a `Lock` gives a race-free count of completed tasks.

## Complexity
O(N) total work for N tasks spread across W threads, so wall-clock ≈ O(N/W * task_time); space O(N) for queued tasks and results.

## Pitfalls
- Using a blocking `get()` without timeout makes the shutdown event unobservable and workers hang forever.
- Calling `task_done()` more or fewer times than `get()` corrupts `join()` (raises or blocks indefinitely).
- Letting exceptions propagate out of the worker silently kills threads and shrinks the pool.
- Reading results with `empty()` is racy in general; here it is safe only because all workers have already been joined before `get_results`.

## Summary
Limit the number of concurrent workers to a fixed maximum while processing many independent jobs (e.g. fetching 10 URLs with at most 3 in flight). Input is a list of jobs; output is the aggregated result per job. The construct must block extra workers until a slot frees up.

## Why it matters
A counting semaphore is the canonical primitive for rate-limiting concurrency: bounding open connections, DB pool size, or API calls. In Go it is idiomatically expressed as a buffered channel; in Rust (std only) you build it from a Mutex + Condvar.

## Idea
- In Go, a buffered channel `sema` of capacity N acts as a permit pool: sending before launching a goroutine acquires a permit (blocks when full), and a deferred receive releases it.
- A `sync.WaitGroup` tracks all launched goroutines so `main` waits for completion; shared output is guarded by a `sync.Mutex` since maps are not concurrency-safe.
- In Rust, `Semaphore` holds a count behind a `Mutex` and a `Condvar`: `acquire` waits while count >= max, then increments; `release` decrements and notifies one waiter.
- The semaphore is shared across threads via `Arc`; `notify_one` wakes exactly one blocked acquirer to keep throughput at the cap.

## Complexity
With M jobs and cap K, wall-clock ≈ O(ceil(M/K) * job_time); space O(K) permits plus O(M) for results/handles.

## Pitfalls
- Forgetting to release the permit (no defer / no `release`) leaks slots and eventually deadlocks.
- Acquiring inside the goroutine instead of before launching lets all goroutines start, defeating the limit; in Go acquire before `go`.
- In Rust, using `if` instead of `while` around the Condvar wait is wrong because of spurious wakeups.
- Writing to a shared map/result store without a mutex is a data race.

## Summary
Build a data-processing pipeline where each stage is a goroutine/thread connected by channels: a generator emits values, intermediate stages transform them (square, double, filter, multiply), and a consumer reads the final stream. Input is a list of integers; output is the transformed stream printed in order.

## Why it matters
The pipeline pattern decouples stages, enables natural streaming and backpressure, and lets each stage run concurrently. It underlies ETL flows, stream processors, and any staged transform where you want composition without buffering everything in memory.

## Idea
- Each stage is a function that takes an input channel and returns a new output channel, launching a goroutine that ranges over the input, transforms each value, and sends to the output.
- Closing the output channel with `defer close(out)` when the input drains propagates termination downstream, so the final `range` loop ends cleanly.
- Stage signatures must take a receive-only channel (`<-chan int`), not a plain `int`, so stages compose; the transform body must be a complete expression (e.g. `v * 2`).
- In Rust the analog uses `mpsc` channels: dropping the sender when a stage's input iterator finishes closes the channel; `tee` fans out by sending to two senders, and `merge` fans in by cloning a sender across two reader threads.

## Complexity
O(N) total elements flow through each of S stages, so O(N*S) work; space is O(S) channels with O(1) buffered items per stage (bounded memory streaming).

## Pitfalls
- Forgetting to close (Go) or drop (Rust) the output sender leaves the downstream consumer blocked forever.
- A wrong stage signature (value instead of channel) or an incomplete expression like `v *` will not compile.
- In a tee/merge fan-out, an unbalanced sender clone count means the merged channel never closes.
- Unbuffered channels give lockstep behavior; that is correct here but means a slow stage backpressures the whole pipeline.

## Задача
Построить **конвейер** (pipeline) из стадий: каждая стадия читает из входного канала, преобразует значения и пишет в свой выходной канал.

## Что реализовать
- `generate(nums ...int) <-chan int` — источник: шлёт переданные числа и закрывает канал.
- `square(in <-chan int) <-chan int` — возводит каждое значение в квадрат.
- `double(in <-chan int) <-chan int` — умножает каждое значение на 2.

Каждая стадия: своя горутина, `defer close(out)`, `for v := range in`.

## Требования
- Стадии соединяются `generate → square → double`.
- Каждый канал закрывает та стадия, что в него пишет.
- Нет утечек горутин, нет паник на закрытом канале.

## Пример
`generate(1,2,3,4,5)` → square → double → `2, 8, 18, 32, 50`.

## Summary
Wait on two channels simultaneously and react to whichever delivers first, with an overall timeout. Two goroutines send a message after different delays; the main goroutine must print both messages as they arrive and bail out if neither responds within a deadline.

## Why it matters
`select` is Go's core primitive for multiplexing concurrent events: handling multiple sources, implementing timeouts/cancellation, and avoiding blocking on a single channel. It is the building block for fan-in, request deadlines, and graceful shutdown.

## Idea
- `select` blocks until one of its `case` communications is ready, then executes that case; if several are ready it picks one at random.
- A loop runs `select` repeatedly (here until `done == 2`) so both messages are consumed across iterations rather than only the first.
- A `case <-time.After(d)` arm provides a timeout: if no real channel fires within the duration, the timer channel becomes ready and the code exits.
- This works because each delayed sender becomes ready independently, and `select` lets the receiver respond to them in arrival order without busy-waiting.

## Complexity
O(K) iterations for K expected messages; space O(1) aside from the timer channel and goroutines.

## Pitfalls
- A fresh `time.After` is created each loop iteration, so the timeout effectively resets per message; for a single overall deadline use one timer or a context.
- Without the loop, `select` fires once and the second message is lost; the senders may then block on unbuffered channels.
- A `default` case would turn the select non-blocking and cause a busy spin.
- Unbuffered sender goroutines leak if the receiver exits early (e.g. on timeout) and never drains them.

# Задание 11: concurrent.futures — ThreadPool, ProcessPool, as_completed

import time
from concurrent.futures import (
    ThreadPoolExecutor,
    ProcessPoolExecutor,
    as_completed,
    Future,       # Future
    wait,
)
from concurrent.futures import TimeoutError as FuturesTimeoutError

# --- ThreadPoolExecutor: базовое использование ---

def fetch_url(url: str) -> dict:
    """Имитация HTTP-запроса"""
    time.sleep(0.2)
    return {"url": url, "status": 200, "size": len(url) * 100}

def fetch_many_threaded(urls: list[str], max_workers: int = 4) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    with ThreadPoolExecutor( max_workers=max_workers) as executor:
        # submit возвращает Future
        future_to_url = {
            executor.submit(fetch_url, url): url
            for url in urls
        }

        # as_completed — получаем результаты по мере готовности
        for future in as_completed(future_to_url):
            url = future_to_url[future]
            try:
                data = future.result()
                results.append(data)
                print(f"  ✓ {url}: {data['size']}b")
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"  ✗ {url}: {e}")

    return results

# --- executor.map — упрощённый вариант ---

def process_batch(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        results = executor.map(lambda x: x ** 2, items)
        return list(results)

# --- ProcessPoolExecutor: CPU-bound задачи ---

def cpu_heavy(n: int) -> int:
    """Считаем сумму до n (имитация тяжёлой работы)"""
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total += i
    return total

def parallel_compute(numbers: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        futures = [executor.submit(cpu_heavy, n) for n in numbers]

        results = []
        for f in as_completed(futures):
            results.append(f.result())
    return results

# --- Таймаут и отмена ---

def slow_task(seconds: float) -> str:
    time.sleep(seconds)
    return f"done after {seconds}s"

def with_timeout_demo():
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as executor:
        fast = executor.submit(slow_task, 0.1)
        slow = executor.submit(slow_task, 10.0)

        # Получаем с таймаутом
        try:
            result = fast.result(timeout=1.0)
            print(f"  fast: {result}")
        except FuturesTimeoutError:
            print("  fast: timed out")

        # Отменяем медленную задачу
        cancelled = slow.cancel()
        print(f"  slow cancelled: {cancelled}")

# --- wait: ждём первый результат ---

def wait_for_first():
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:
        futures = [
            executor.submit(slow_task, 0.5),
            executor.submit(slow_task, 0.1),
            executor.submit(slow_task, 0.3),
        ]

        done, not_done = wait(futures, return_when="FIRST_COMPLETED")
        print(f"  completed: {len(done)}, pending: {len(not_done)}")

        for f in done:
            print(f"  result: {f.result()}")

        # Ждём остальные
        remaining, _ = wait(not_done)
        print(f"  all done: {len(remaining)}")

# --- Callback на Future ---

def on_complete(future: Future):
    if future.exception() is not None:
        print(f"  [callback] error: {future.exception()}")
    else:
        print(f"  [callback] result: {future.result()}")

def callback_demo():
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as executor:
        f1 = executor.submit(fetch_url, "api/data")
        f1.add_done_callback(on_complete)

        f2 = executor.submit(lambda: 1 / 0)
        f2.add_done_callback(on_complete)

        time.sleep(1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== ThreadPool fetch ===")
    urls = [f"https://api.example.com/{i}" for i in range(6)]
    results = fetch_many_threaded(urls, max_workers=4)
    print(f"total: {len(results)} responses\n")

    print("=== executor.map ===")
    squared = process_batch([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
    print(f"squared: {squared}\n")

    print("=== ProcessPool ===")
    numbers = [10_000_000, 20_000_000, 5_000_000]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    sums = parallel_compute(numbers)
    print(f"sums: {sums}")
    print(f"elapsed: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s\n")

    print("=== Timeout & Cancel ===")
    with_timeout_demo()
    print()

    print("=== Wait first ===")
    wait_for_first()
    print()

    print("=== Callbacks ===")
    callback_demo()

## Summary
Demonstrate Python's `concurrent.futures` high-level API: run I/O-bound work on a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, CPU-bound work on a `ProcessPoolExecutor`, and collect results as they finish with `as_completed`. The functions take lists of inputs (URLs, ints) and return lists of results, plus show timeouts, cancellation, `wait`, and done-callbacks.

## Why it matters
`concurrent.futures` is the standard, ergonomic way to parallelize work in Python without hand-managing threads or the GIL details; the same Future/Executor abstraction switches between threads and processes with one line. It shows up in scrapers, batch ETL, and any fan-out/fan-in workload.

## Idea
- Submit each task with `executor.submit(fn, arg)`, which returns a `Future`; keep a `future -> input` map so you can attribute results.
- Iterate `as_completed(futures)` to process results in completion order rather than submission order, calling `future.result()` (which re-raises worker exceptions).
- Use `ThreadPoolExecutor` for I/O-bound work (releases GIL during blocking calls) and `ProcessPoolExecutor` for CPU-bound work (true parallelism across cores).
- `future.result(timeout=...)` raises `TimeoutError`; `future.cancel()` only succeeds if the task has not started; `wait(..., return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)` blocks until the first completes; `add_done_callback` fires when the Future settles.

## Complexity
Wall-clock time is roughly total_work / min(num_tasks, max_workers); memory is O(num_tasks) for the Future objects and collected results.

## Pitfalls
- `ProcessPoolExecutor` requires the `if __name__ == "__main__"` guard and picklable functions/args; lambdas and closures fail to pickle.
- `executor.map` returns results in input order and re-raises the first exception lazily during iteration, unlike `as_completed`.
- `future.cancel()` returns False once the task is running, so a long task cannot be force-stopped this way.
- Exceptions inside workers are swallowed until you call `.result()` or `.exception()`; forgetting to do so hides failures.

## Summary
Build a generic worker pool in Go using type parameters: a `Generator[T]` that streams a slice onto a channel, and `Workers[T, R]` that fans out `num` goroutines applying `fn func(T) R` and fans the results back into one output channel. Everything respects a `context.Context` for cancellation, and `main` wires them with a 2-second timeout.

## Why it matters
The fan-out/fan-in pipeline is the canonical Go concurrency pattern for bounded parallelism over a stream of work, and generics let you write it once for any input/output type instead of copy-pasting per type. It underpins crawlers, batch processors, and rate-limited API clients.

## Idea
- `Generator` launches a goroutine that pushes each element on `out`, using `select` so a `ctx.Done()` can stop it mid-send without blocking forever.
- `Workers` starts `num` goroutines, each looping on `select` over `ctx.Done()` and a receive from `in`; on a received value it computes `fn(v)` and sends to `out` (again guarded by `ctx.Done()` to avoid a send-block deadlock).
- A `sync.WaitGroup` counts the workers; a separate goroutine `wg.Wait()`s and then `close(out)` so the consumer's `range` terminates exactly once after all workers exit.
- The input parameter must be a receive-only `<-chan T` so the channel returned by `Generator` is assignable.

## Complexity
Time is O(n / num) wall-clock for n items across num workers (plus per-item `fn` cost); space is O(num) goroutines plus small channel buffers.

## Pitfalls
- The original used `context.Context(...)` (a type, not callable) instead of `context.WithTimeout`, and declared `in chan T` instead of `<-chan T`, neither of which compiles.
- Only the goroutine that owns `out` may close it; closing from a worker would panic on a second close. Here a single closer goroutine after `wg.Wait()` is correct.
- Without the `ctx.Done()` case on the output send, a cancelled consumer would leak blocked worker goroutines.
- Forgetting `defer cancel()` leaks the context's timer.

## Summary
Implement a minimal hand-rolled equivalent of `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup`: an `ErrGroup` that launches functions with `Go(func() error)`, captures the first error, cancels a shared context on failure, and reports that error from `Wait()`. The demo runs five `fetchData` calls where one fails and verifies the group still completes cleanly.

## Why it matters
errgroup is the idiomatic way to run a set of related goroutines, propagate the first failure, and cancel the rest — far cleaner than juggling raw `WaitGroup` + error channels by hand. Understanding its internals (WaitGroup, a guarded error, a cancel func) is a common Go interview and real-world need.

## Idea
- The struct holds a `sync.WaitGroup`, a `sync.Mutex` guarding the first `err`, and a derived `ctx`/`cancel` from `context.WithCancel`.
- `Go` does `wg.Add(1)` then runs the function in a goroutine; on a non-nil error it locks, records the error only if none was stored yet (first-error-wins), unlocks, and calls `cancel()` to signal siblings.
- `Wait` blocks on `wg.Wait()`, then calls `cancel()` to release context resources unconditionally, and returns the stored error.
- The mutex is essential because multiple goroutines may fail concurrently and race on the `err` field.

## Complexity
Time is bounded by the slowest goroutine (they run concurrently); space is O(g) for g in-flight goroutines plus a single error and cancel func.

## Pitfalls
- Reading/writing `g.err` without the mutex is a data race; the "store only if nil" check must be inside the locked section.
- Worker functions must actually observe `g.ctx.Done()` to benefit from cancellation; cancelling a context cannot forcibly stop a goroutine that ignores it.
- Always call `cancel()` in `Wait` (even on success) to avoid leaking the context.
- This minimal version does not bound concurrency the way `errgroup.SetLimit` does.

## Summary
Build two reusable Go concurrency primitives: an `orDone` wrapper that relays values from an input channel but stops the moment `ctx` is cancelled, and `mergeWithCtx` that fans several `<-chan int` sources into one output channel, again honoring context cancellation. `main` runs three number generators under a 500ms timeout and prints the interleaved, merged stream until cancellation closes everything.

## Why it matters
`orDone` removes the repetitive nested `select { case v := <-in; case <-ctx.Done() }` boilerplate, and context-aware fan-in is the standard way to combine multiple producers while guaranteeing no goroutine leaks on cancellation or timeout. This pattern appears in pipelines, event aggregators, and streaming APIs.

## Idea
- `orDone` loops on a `select` over `ctx.Done()` and a receive from `in`; on a received value it does an inner `select` to either forward it or bail on cancellation, and closes its `out` when `in` closes or the context ends.
- `mergeWithCtx` adds `len(chans)` to a `WaitGroup`, then starts one goroutine per source that ranges over `orDone(ctx, c)` and forwards each value to the shared `out` (guarded by `ctx.Done()`).
- A separate goroutine calls `wg.Wait()` and then `close(out)` exactly once, so the consumer's `range merged` terminates after every source drains or the context fires.
- Generators also select on `ctx.Done()` for every send, so a timeout unblocks any goroutine parked on a send.

## Complexity
Time is the duration of the slowest still-running source (capped by the context timeout); space is O(k) goroutines for k merged channels plus unbuffered channel handoffs.

## Pitfalls
- The closing goroutine must call `wg.Wait()` (not `wg.Done()`); calling `Done` instead corrupts the counter and closes `out` immediately, causing a premature/garbled stream and a likely "send on closed channel" panic — this was the original bug.
- `main` must build the context with `context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), ...)`, not `context.Context(...)`, which does not compile.
- Every send to `out` needs the `ctx.Done()` escape, or a cancelled consumer leaves producers blocked forever (goroutine leak).
- Only the dedicated closer may `close(out)`; closing from worker goroutines would double-close and panic.

## Summary
Implement a thread-safe bounded (fixed-capacity) FIFO queue of ints with `Enqueue`, `Dequeue`, and `Len`. `Enqueue` must block when the queue is full; `Dequeue` must block when it is empty. Multiple producer and consumer goroutines use it concurrently, and the program must terminate without deadlock once every produced item has been consumed.

## Why it matters
Bounded blocking queues are the backbone of producer/consumer systems, work pools, and back-pressure: they cap memory while letting fast producers slow down to match slow consumers. The condition-variable pattern here is the classic way to coordinate "wait until a predicate holds" in Go when a plain channel does not fit.

## Idea
- Guard the slice `items` with a single `sync.Mutex`.
- Use two `sync.Cond` instances sharing that mutex: `notFull` (signaled after a dequeue frees space) and `notEmpty` (signaled after an enqueue adds data).
- `Enqueue` loops `for len(items) >= cap { notFull.Wait() }`, appends, then `notEmpty.Signal()`.
- `Dequeue` loops `for len(items) == 0 { notEmpty.Wait() }`, pops the front, then `notFull.Signal()`.
- The `for` (not `if`) around `Wait` is essential because `Wait` releases the lock and a woken goroutine must re-check the predicate against possible spurious or racing wakeups.

## Complexity
Each `Enqueue`/`Dequeue` is O(1) amortized work under the lock (front removal via reslice); space is O(capacity). Concurrency is bounded by the single mutex, with condition variables parking blocked goroutines instead of busy-waiting.

## Pitfalls
- Using `if` instead of `for` around `cond.Wait()` — a thread can wake to find the predicate no longer true and corrupt state.
- Forgetting to hold the mutex while calling `Wait`/`Signal`; `Wait` must be called with the lock held.
- Mismatched total enqueues vs dequeues causes a permanent block: here 3×5 produced must equal 2×7 + 1 consumed.
- `items = items[1:]` keeps the backing array from shrinking; fine for a drill but can leak memory in long-running queues (use a ring buffer instead).

## Summary
Build a four-stage channel pipeline `gen -> filter -> square -> sink` over the integers 1..20, where `filter` keeps even numbers and `square` squares them. Every stage must respect a `context.Context` with a timeout so the whole pipeline shuts down cleanly on cancellation or when the source is exhausted.

## Why it matters
Staged channel pipelines are the idiomatic Go way to stream and transform data with natural back-pressure, and threading a `context` through every stage is the standard cancellation/timeout discipline used in servers, ETL, and stream processors.

## Idea
- Each stage is a function that takes the upstream `<-chan int` plus `ctx` and returns a new `<-chan int`, running its own goroutine that `defer close(out)`.
- Inside each stage, every blocking operation is wrapped in a `select` with a `case <-ctx.Done(): return`, so cancellation is honored both while reading from `in` and while writing to `out`.
- Detecting upstream completion uses the two-value receive `v, ok := <-in`; when `ok` is false the stage returns, which closes its own output and cascades shutdown downstream.
- The final `sink` ranges (via select) until either the channel closes or the context is done.

## Complexity
Time is O(n) for n source items across the stages; space is O(1) per stage plus the goroutine stacks (one goroutine per stage). Channels are unbuffered, so throughput is gated by the slowest stage.

## Pitfalls
- Selecting on `ctx.Done()` only when reading but not when writing (or vice versa) leaves a goroutine blocked on a full/empty channel after cancel — a goroutine leak.
- Forgetting `defer close(out)` breaks the close-cascade and hangs downstream `range`/receives.
- Not calling `cancel()` (here via `defer cancel()`) leaks the context's timer.
- Closing a channel from the receiving side, or from multiple senders, panics; only the owning stage closes its output.

## Summary
Several producer goroutines emit random ints (with duplicates) onto a `raw` channel; a pool of deduplicator goroutines forwards only first-seen values onto a `unique` channel; a collector gathers them into a slice. The output is the set of distinct values produced, with no data races and a clean, ordered shutdown.

## Why it matters
"Concurrent generate then deduplicate" models real fan-in/dedup pipelines (event ingestion, crawler URL frontiers, ID minting). It exercises the two core Go safety tools — a mutex-protected shared set and a disciplined channel-close ordering — that prevent both races and "send on closed channel" panics.

## Idea
- A `SafeSet` wraps `map[int]struct{}` with a `sync.RWMutex`; `Add` takes the write lock and returns `true` only the first time a value is seen, giving an atomic test-and-insert.
- Producers write to a buffered `raw` channel and finish; their `prodWg` is awaited before `close(raw)`.
- Multiple deduplicators `range` over `raw` and forward novel values to `unique`; their `dedupWg` is awaited before `close(unique)`.
- The collector `range`s `unique`, appending under its own mutex, and closes a `done` channel when finished; `main` waits on `done`.
- The strict close order (producers → raw → dedups → unique → collector → done) is what guarantees no send happens on a closed channel.

## Complexity
Time is O(N) for N produced items (each is one O(1) average map op under the lock); space is O(U) for U unique values. Parallelism is limited by lock contention on the single set mutex.

## Pitfalls
- Closing `raw` or `unique` before its writers' WaitGroup has returned causes a panic on a send to a closed channel.
- The dedup test-and-insert must be one locked operation; a separate "contains then add" allows two goroutines to both pass and emit a duplicate.
- Using `RLock` for `Add` would be a data race since it mutates the map; only `Len` may use the read lock.
- Forgetting the collector's own mutex when appending to the shared slice is a race even though only one collector runs here (defensive and required if scaled to many collectors).

## Задача
Несколько продюсеров шлют (возможно повторяющиеся) числа; дедупликаторы пропускают только **впервые встреченные**; коллектор собирает результат. Всё конкурентно и потокобезопасно.

## Что реализовать
- `type SafeSet` на `sync.RWMutex`: `Add(val int) bool` (`true`, если значение добавлено впервые), `Len() int`.
- `producer(out chan<- int, count, maxVal int, wg *sync.WaitGroup)` — шлёт `count` случайных чисел из `[0, maxVal)`.
- `deduplicator(in <-chan int, out chan<- int, set *SafeSet, wg *sync.WaitGroup)` — пропускает в `out` только новые значения (по `set.Add`).
- `collector(in <-chan int, results *[]int, mu *sync.Mutex, done chan struct{})` — собирает значения в срез; по закрытии входа закрывает `done`.

## Требования
- Никаких гонок: `SafeSet` под `RWMutex`, общий срез — под `Mutex`.
- Правильная **последовательность закрытия** каналов: `raw` после всех продюсеров, `unique` после всех дедупликаторов; затем ждать `collector` через `<-done`.
- Отсутствие deadlock.

## Пример
4 продюсера × 50 значений, `maxVal=20` → уникальных значений не больше 20.

problems.info:
## Summary
Assemble a cancelable concurrency pipeline from three reusable stages: `Generator` streams a slice onto a channel; `processParallel` runs a worker pool that doubles each value; `merge` fans in several channels into one. `main` wires two generators through worker pools and merges them, printing every result, all under a 5-second `context` timeout.

## Why it matters
This is the canonical Go concurrency toolkit — generator, fan-out worker pool, fan-in merge, plus context cancellation — composed end to end. The same three primitives appear in crawlers, batch processors, and any service that parallelizes a stream of work while staying cancelable.

## Idea
- `Generator`: a goroutine sends each element via a `select` over `out <- v` and `<-ctx.Done()`, then `defer close(out)`.
- `processParallel`: spawn `workers` goroutines, each reading `v, ok := <-in` and sending `v*2`, every channel op guarded by `ctx.Done()`. A `sync.WaitGroup` tracks the workers; a separate goroutine does `wg.Wait()` then `close(out)` so the output closes exactly once after all workers stop.
- `merge`: one goroutine per input channel forwards values to `out`, guarded by ctx; a `wg.Wait()`-then-`close(out)` goroutine closes the merged output. The loop variable is passed as a parameter `go func(c <-chan int)` to avoid the classic capture bug.
- `main` ranges over `merged`; the chain of closes propagates termination upward to downward.

## Complexity
Time is O(N) total for N input items (each doubled once, forwarded twice through stages); space is O(workers + channels) goroutines plus unbuffered channel handoff. Throughput scales with the worker count up to the slowest stage.

## Pitfalls
- Capturing the range variable directly in the merge goroutine (instead of passing it as an argument) makes all goroutines read the same channel — a real bug pre-Go 1.22.
- Closing `out` from a worker rather than from the single `wg.Wait()` goroutine causes "close of closed channel" panics when there are multiple workers.
- Omitting `ctx.Done()` on the send side leaves goroutines blocked after timeout, leaking them.
- Forgetting `defer cancel()` leaks the timeout timer even though the pipeline finishes early.

## Задача
Собрать полный конвейер из трёх переиспользуемых стадий с поддержкой `context`: **Generator** (источник) → **processParallel** (worker pool) → **merge** (fan-in), и `main`, который их соединяет.

## Что реализовать
- `Generator(ctx context.Context, data []int) <-chan int` — шлёт `data` в канал, закрывает его, уважает `ctx`.
- `processParallel(ctx context.Context, in <-chan int, workers int) <-chan int` — пул воркеров; каждый считает `result = v * 2`; `out` закрывается после завершения всех (через `sync.WaitGroup`).
- `merge(ctx context.Context, channels ...<-chan int) <-chan int` — fan-in нескольких каналов в один, с отменой по `ctx`.
- `main` — два генератора → два `processParallel` (по 3 воркера) → `merge` → печать; общий таймаут 5с.

## Требования
- Все отправки/чтения — под `select` с `ctx.Done()`.
- Каждый `out` закрывается ровно один раз той стадией, что в него пишет.
- Передавай переменную канала в горутину аргументом (без захвата переменной цикла).
- Без deadlock и утечек горутин.

## Пример
`[1..5]` и `[6..10]`, каждое значение ×2, слияние → 10 чисел в произвольном порядке, затем `done`.

problems.t: Конкурентный доступ к map с RWMutex
problems.desc: Конкурентный доступ к map с RWMutex
problems.info:
## Summary
Build a map that is safely shared across many goroutines/threads. The program spawns N concurrent writers that populate the map, waits for them, then spawns N concurrent readers, and finally reports the map size. Output is the final element count (and, in the Rust variant, sample lookups).

## Why it matters
Go maps and most language hash maps are not safe for concurrent writes; an unguarded concurrent map write panics or corrupts state. Guarding shared state with a read-write lock is the foundational pattern behind in-memory caches, registries, and session stores.

## Idea
- Wrap the map with a `sync.RWMutex` (Go) / `RwLock` (Rust).
- Take the exclusive write lock (`Lock` / `write()`) around every mutation so only one writer touches the map at a time.
- Take the shared read lock (`RLock` / `read()`) around lookups so many readers can proceed in parallel while no writer holds the lock.
- A `sync.WaitGroup` (Go) or joining thread handles (Rust) ensures all writers finish before reads begin and that `main` does not exit early.
- The RWMutex is correct because writes are mutually exclusive with everything, while concurrent reads of immutable data are harmless.

## Complexity
O(N) total work for N operations, each lock acquire/release is O(1); space O(N) for the stored entries plus O(1) lock overhead. Concurrency is bounded by lock contention: writers serialize, readers run in parallel.

## Pitfalls
- Method name is `RLock`, not `Rlock`; the lowercase variant does not compile.
- Capture the loop variable per iteration (`i := i`) or every goroutine sees the same final `i`.
- Forgetting `wg.Wait()` (or joining handles) lets `main` exit before goroutines finish, losing writes or causing a data race.
- Never read or write the map outside the lock, even for a "harmless" length check.

## Summary
Implement a LIFO stack supporting push, pop, peek/top, and emptiness check. The Go version stores strings; the Rust version is generic over `T` with an optional capacity limit and typed errors. Output is the sequence of pushes, peeks, and pops demonstrating last-in-first-out order.

## Why it matters
The stack is one of the most reused abstractions in software: call frames, expression evaluation, undo history, backtracking, DFS, and balanced-bracket checks all rely on it. Knowing how to back it with a dynamic array is interview-table-stakes.

## Idea
- Back the stack with a growable slice (`[]string`) or `Vec<T>`; the end of the array is the top.
- `Push` appends to the end in amortized O(1).
- `Pop` removes and returns the last element, signaling emptiness via an `ok` bool (Go) or `Result`/`Option` (Rust).
- `Top`/`peek` returns the last element without removing it.
- The Rust variant adds a `max_size` for overflow detection, a `From<Vec>` constructor, and an `Iterator` impl that drains from the top.

## Complexity
Push/pop/peek are amortized O(1) time (occasional O(n) reallocation on growth); space O(n) for n stored items.

## Pitfalls
- Always check emptiness before indexing `items[len-1]` to avoid an index-out-of-range panic.
- Re-slicing on pop (`items[:len-1]`) keeps the backing array; the dropped element is not zeroed, which can retain references in pointer-typed stacks.
- In Rust, the `Iterator` impl consumes the stack by value, so you cannot reuse it afterward.
- A bounded stack must reject pushes once `len >= max_size` rather than silently growing.

## Summary
Build a thread-safe key/value cache that scales under concurrent access by splitting storage into N independent shards. A key is hashed to choose a shard, and only that shard's lock is taken. Output demonstrates parallel writes/reads and a successful lookup of a stored key.

## Why it matters
A single global mutex around a shared map becomes a contention bottleneck under high concurrency. Sharding (lock striping) is the standard scaling trick used by concurrent hash maps, connection pools, and in-memory caches to let unrelated keys proceed in parallel.

## Idea
- Create an array of shards, each holding its own `map`/`HashMap` guarded by its own `sync.RWMutex` / `RwLock`.
- For each operation, hash the key (FNV in Go, `DefaultHasher` in Rust) and reduce it modulo the shard count to pick a shard.
- Lock only the selected shard, so operations on keys landing in different shards never block each other.
- Use the write lock for `Set`/`insert`/`delete` and the read lock for `Get`, maximizing read parallelism.
- Distribution quality depends on the hash spreading keys roughly uniformly across shards.

## Complexity
O(1) average per operation (hash + single-shard map access); space O(total entries) plus O(numShards) lock overhead. Expected contention drops by roughly a factor of numShards versus one global lock.

## Pitfalls
- Computing the shard index as `int(h.Sum64()) % n` is a bug: converting a large `uint64` to `int` can yield a negative value, and Go's `%` keeps the sign, producing a negative index and a panic. Do the modulo in unsigned arithmetic: `int(h.Sum64() % uint64(n))`.
- A non-power-of-two shard count is fine with modulo, but masking (`& (n-1)`) only works when n is a power of two.
- Cross-shard operations like total `len()`/`keys()` are not a consistent snapshot; entries can change between shard reads.
- Capturing the loop variable in the writer goroutine is required (`func(i int)` or `i := i`).

## Summary
Implement a singly linked list of integer nodes supporting PushFront, PushBack, PopFront, Find, and Print, while tracking Size. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; the list keeps a head pointer. Output shows the list contents after insertions and a front removal.

## Why it matters
Linked lists are the canonical pointer-manipulation exercise and underpin queues, adjacency lists, LRU caches, and any structure needing O(1) head insertion without array reallocation. They sharpen reasoning about nil/null pointers and aliasing.

## Idea
- A `Node` has a `Value` and a `Next` pointer; the `LinkedList` holds `Head` and a `Size` counter.
- `PushFront` allocates a node whose `Next` is the current head, then makes it the new head — O(1).
- `PushBack` walks from head following `Next` until the last node and links the new node there; an empty list sets head directly.
- `PopFront` returns the head value and advances head to `Head.Next`, signaling emptiness with an `ok` bool.
- `Find` and `Print` traverse linearly from head until the `nil` terminator.

## Complexity
PushFront and PopFront are O(1); PushBack, Find, and Print are O(n) because they traverse to the tail/match. Space is O(n) for n nodes.

## Pitfalls
- Handle the empty-list case in PushBack (head is nil) before dereferencing `current.Next`.
- PopFront on an empty list must return the not-ok flag instead of dereferencing a nil head.
- Keep `Size` consistent with every mutation, or it drifts from the real count.
- Without a tail pointer, repeated PushBack is O(n) each; add a tail field if frequent appends are needed.

problems.t: Паттерны проектирования — Singleton, Observer, Strategy, Chain of Responsibility
problems.desc: Паттерны проектирования — Singleton, Observer, Strategy, Chain of Responsibility
problems.info:
## Summary
Implement and demonstrate four classic design patterns in Python: Singleton (both via `__new__` and via a decorator), Chain of Responsibility, and Strategy. The "input" is a series of requests/data items; the output is the processed result produced by routing them through a chain of handlers or applying a swappable strategy function.

## Why it matters
These patterns are the vocabulary of object-oriented design: Singleton centralizes shared config, Chain of Responsibility models middleware pipelines (auth, rate limiting, logging), and Strategy decouples an algorithm from its caller. They show up directly in web frameworks, request pipelines, and pluggable processing code.

## Idea
- Singleton via `__new__` caches the single instance in a class attribute and returns it on every construction; note `__init__` still runs each time, so the stored value reflects the last constructor call.
- Singleton via decorator wraps the class in a closure that memoizes instances in a dict keyed by class, returning the cached one.
- Chain of Responsibility: each `Handler` holds a reference to the next handler; `set_next` returns the next handler so links can be fluently chained, and each handler either short-circuits with an error or calls `pass_next` to delegate.
- Strategy: `Processor` stores a callable and `process` simply invokes it; swapping behavior is just reassigning the callable, which works because functions are first-class objects.

## Complexity
Singleton lookup is O(1); a chain of n handlers processes one request in O(n); Strategy dispatch is O(1) plus the cost of the chosen function. Space is O(1) for singletons and O(n) for the handler chain.

## Pitfalls
- Singleton via `__new__` does not prevent `__init__` from re-running, so mutable state can be silently overwritten on each call.
- The `__new__`/decorator singletons are not thread-safe; concurrent first construction can create two instances without a lock.
- Forgetting to return the next handler from `set_next` breaks fluent chaining; forgetting to call `pass_next` silently drops the request.
- Strategy functions must share the same signature, or swapping them at runtime will raise at call time.

## Summary
Define a `Shape` interface (`Area`, `Perimeter`, `Name`) in Go and implement it for `Rectangle`, `Circle`, and `Triangle`. A factory `NewShape` builds a concrete shape from a kind string plus parameters, and a polymorphic `PrintInfo` prints any shape's name, area, and perimeter.

## Why it matters
Interfaces are Go's primary abstraction mechanism: they let you write code against behavior instead of concrete types. A factory plus interface is the standard way to construct one of several implementations chosen at runtime, common in plugin systems, parsers, and config-driven object creation.

## Idea
- Declare `Shape` as a set of methods; any type whose value receivers define all three methods implicitly satisfies it.
- Each struct implements the geometry: rectangle is width times height, circle uses pi r squared, triangle uses Heron's formula via half the perimeter.
- `NewShape` validates the parameter count per kind and returns the concrete struct as a `Shape` interface value, or an error for bad input.
- `PrintInfo` accepts the interface, so it works uniformly for every shape via dynamic dispatch.

## Complexity
All area/perimeter computations are O(1) time and O(1) space; iterating and printing a slice of n shapes is O(n).

## Pitfalls
- Returning `nil` as a `Shape` from the factory on error must be paired with a non-nil error, and callers must check the error before using the value.
- Heron's formula returns NaN for invalid triangles where a side exceeds the sum of the others; validate the triangle inequality if correctness matters.
- All methods use value receivers, so they must be consistent; mixing pointer and value receivers can make a type fail to satisfy the interface for value instances.
- The factory's parameter-count checks are the only guard against malformed input; missing them causes index-out-of-range panics.

problems.desc: В Go нет классов и наследования. Вместо этого — встраивание структур. Встроенная структура "продвигает" свои поля и методы наверх.
problems.info:
## Summary
Demonstrate Go struct embedding as a substitute for inheritance. `Entity` is embedded in `User`, which is embedded in `Admin`; embedded fields and methods are promoted to the outer type, and each level can override `String()`. The program prints promoted fields and the correctly dispatched `String()` output.

## Why it matters
Go has no classes or inheritance; embedding is how you reuse and compose behavior. It powers idioms like embedding `sync.Mutex`, wrapping `io.Reader`, or layering domain types, and understanding method promotion versus overriding is a frequent interview topic.

## Idea
- Embedding a type with no field name promotes its exported fields and methods to the outer struct, so `admin.ID` reaches `Entity.ID` through two levels.
- When the outer type defines a method with the same name (`String`), it shadows the promoted one; the outer method can still call the inner via the qualified path `u.Entity.String()`.
- Because `User` and `Admin` each define `String()`, they satisfy `fmt.Stringer`, so `fmt.Println` invokes their custom formatting.
- This is composition, not inheritance: there is no polymorphic substitutability of `Admin` for `User` unless an interface is involved.

## Complexity
Field and method promotion is resolved at compile time, so access is O(1); `HasPermission` scans the permissions slice in O(n).

## Pitfalls
- Method promotion is not virtual dispatch: a method on `Entity` that calls `String()` would call `Entity.String()`, not the outer override, since Go embedding has no dynamic binding to the outer type.
- Ambiguous field/method names at the same embedding depth cause a compile error; the shallowest name wins only when depths differ.
- An embedded value type cannot be assigned to a variable of the outer type's interface unless the methods are present at that level.
- Forgetting to qualify (`u.Entity.String()`) inside the override causes infinite recursion if you accidentally call the promoted name.

problems.desc: Интерфейс в Go — набор методов. Любой тип, у которого есть эти методы, автоматически реализует интерфейс (неявная реализация, duck typing).
problems.info:
## Summary
Define a `Shape` interface (`Area`, `Perimeter`, `String`) and implement it for `Circle`, `Rectangle`, and `Triangle`. Demonstrate polymorphism by printing a slice of shapes, summing their areas, and inspecting concrete types with a type assertion and a type switch.

## Why it matters
Implicit interface satisfaction (duck typing) is central to Go: a type implements an interface just by having the right methods, with no explicit declaration. Type assertions and type switches are the standard way to recover concrete behavior from interface values, used everywhere in decoders, error handling, and visitor-style dispatch.

## Idea
- `Shape` lists three methods; each struct satisfies it implicitly by defining all three with value receivers.
- `printShapeInfo` and `totalArea` operate on the interface, so adding a new shape type requires no changes to them, which is the polymorphism payoff.
- A type assertion `s.(Circle)` with the comma-ok form safely tests whether the dynamic type is `Circle` without panicking.
- A type switch `s.(type)` branches on the concrete dynamic type, binding `v` to the typed value in each case.

## Complexity
Each area/perimeter is O(1); `totalArea` over n shapes is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Type assertion and type switch are O(1).

## Pitfalls
- A type assertion without the comma-ok form panics if the dynamic type does not match; always use `v, ok := s.(T)` when unsure.
- Implementing `String()` makes the type a `fmt.Stringer`, so `%s` and `Println` use it; an accidental recursive call inside `String()` causes a stack overflow.
- Value vs pointer receivers must be consistent, or the value form may not satisfy the interface.
- Heron's formula yields NaN for degenerate triangles; the type switch must list every case you care about or fall through silently.

problems.desc: Стратегия — поведение передаётся как интерфейс. Можно менять алгоритм на лету без изменения основного кода.
problems.info:
## Summary
Implement the Strategy pattern in Go: define a `SortStrategy` interface (`Sort([]string)` + `Name()`) with interchangeable implementations (alphabetical, by length, reverse), plus a `Sorter` context that holds a strategy and can swap it at runtime via `SetStrategy`. A parallel `FilterStrategy` interface shows filtering by minimum length or by substring. Input is a slice of strings; output is the slice sorted/filtered according to the currently selected strategy.

## Why it matters
The Strategy pattern lets you select an algorithm at runtime and decouple it from the code that uses it, which is exactly how `sort.Sort` / `sort.Interface`, `http.Handler`, and pluggable comparators work in real Go codebases.

## Idea
- Express the varying behavior (sorting, filtering) as a small interface rather than a hardcoded function.
- Concrete types (`AlphaSort`, `LengthSort`, `ReversSort`) each satisfy the interface; the `Sorter` context depends only on the interface, not the concrete type.
- Swapping the algorithm is just assigning a different value to the `strategy` field, with no change to `Sorter` itself.
- This works because Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so any type with the right methods is a drop-in strategy.

## Complexity
Sorting strategies are O(n log n) time, O(1)/O(log n) auxiliary; filters are O(n·m) time (m = match cost) and O(n) space for the result slice.

## Pitfalls
- `sort.Slice` is not stable; equal-key elements (same length) may keep arbitrary relative order, so do not assert exact ordering of ties.
- `Sort` mutates the underlying slice in place; the caller shares that backing array.
- Comparing reverse order with `>` gives descending lexicographic order, which is not the same as reversing an ascending sort when ties exist.
- Filters should allocate a new slice rather than modifying the input to avoid surprising aliasing.

problems.desc: Декоратор оборачивает объект, добавляя поведение без изменения исходного кода. В Go — через встраивание интерфейса в структуру.
problems.info:
## Summary
Implement the Decorator pattern in Go using interface embedding: a `Logger` interface with `Log(msg)`, a base `SimpleLogger`, and decorators (`TimestampLogger`, `LevelLogger`, `UpperLogger`, `FilterLogger`) that each embed a `Logger`, transform the message, and delegate to the wrapped logger. The input is a log message; the output is that message after passing through the chain of decorators (timestamp prefix, level prefix, uppercasing, or substring filtering).

## Why it matters
Decorators add behavior to an object without modifying it or subclassing, which is how middleware chains (`http.Handler` wrappers), `io.Reader`/`io.Writer` wrappers, and logging pipelines are built in production Go.

## Idea
- Each decorator struct embeds the `Logger` interface, so it automatically satisfies `Logger` and holds a reference to the next logger in the chain.
- The decorator overrides `Log`, does its transformation, then calls the embedded `Logger.Log`, forwarding down the chain.
- Wrapping is composable: you nest constructors to build an arbitrary pipeline, and order matters because each layer sees the output of the layer it wraps.
- The base `SimpleLogger` terminates the chain by actually printing.

## Complexity
O(k) time per log call where k is the number of decorators in the chain (each does O(len(msg)) work); O(k) space for the nested wrapper objects.

## Pitfalls
- Order of nesting changes the result: uppercasing before vs. after adding a level/timestamp prefix produces different strings.
- If a decorator forgets to call the embedded `Logger.Log`, the message is silently dropped (intentional for `FilterLogger`, a bug elsewhere).
- Embedding the interface (not a concrete type) is what keeps decorators interchangeable; embedding a concrete logger would break the chain.
- A nil embedded `Logger` panics on delegation, so always set the wrapped logger.

problems.desc: Наблюдатель — подписчики получают уведомления при изменении состояния.
problems.info:
## Summary
Implement the Observer pattern in Go: a `Publisher` (`Store`) maintains a list of `Observer`s and notifies them on state changes (`AddProduct`, `UpdatePrice`) by calling `OnEvent(event, data)`. Concrete observers (`EmailNotifier`, `DashboardWidget`, `PriceWatcher`) react differently, e.g. `PriceWatcher` raises an alert only when a watched product's new price exceeds its threshold. Input is a series of store mutations; output is the side-effects each subscribed observer emits.

## Why it matters
Observer decouples event producers from consumers and underlies pub/sub systems, UI event handlers, and reactive state propagation; in Go it is the conceptual basis for channel fan-out and event buses.

## Idea
- The subject stores observers as a slice of the `Observer` interface and iterates it on every change, calling `OnEvent`.
- Events carry a name plus a `data any` payload (here a `map[string]any`); observers type-assert and inspect the fields they care about.
- `Subscribe`/`Unsubscribe` add/remove from the slice; removal compares interface values with `==`, which is valid because the concrete observer types are comparable structs.
- Decoupling works because the store depends only on the interface, so new observer types need no change to the publisher.

## Complexity
Notify is O(n) per event over n observers; Unsubscribe is O(n) for the linear search and slice splice; space is O(n) for the observer list.

## Pitfalls
- Comparing observers with `==` panics if any concrete observer type is not comparable (e.g. contains a slice/map field); use an explicit ID or pointer identity instead.
- Mutating the observers slice while iterating in `Notify` (an observer that unsubscribes during notification) can skip or double-process entries.
- Type assertions on the `any` payload must use the comma-ok form; a wrong key or type otherwise yields a zero value silently.
- Reading a missing key in the products map returns the zero `float64`, so `old_price` may be 0 for a never-seen product.

problems.desc: Functional Options — идиоматичный Go-паттерн для конфигурации. Вместо длинного конструктора или builder — передаём функции-опции.
problems.info:
## Summary
Implement two idiomatic Go construction patterns. Functional Options: `NewServer(host, opts...)` starts from sensible defaults and applies a variadic list of `Option` functions (`WithPort`, `WithTLS`, `WithTimeouts`, `WithMaxConns`) that each mutate the `Server`. Factory: `NewStorage(kind)` returns a `Storage` interface implementation (`MemoryStorage` or `DiskStorage`) selected by string, or an error for unknown kinds. Input is a host plus option functions / a storage kind; output is a configured `*Server` or a `Storage` value.

## Why it matters
Functional options give clean, backward-compatible, optional configuration without telescoping constructors or builders, and the factory hides concrete types behind an interface; both are pervasive in real Go libraries (gRPC, zap, database clients).

## Idea
- An `Option` is a `func(*Server)`; each `WithX` returns a closure capturing its argument and setting one field.
- The constructor seeds defaults first, then loops over the options applying them in order, so later options override earlier ones.
- The factory switches on the kind string and returns the matching concrete type as the `Storage` interface, returning an error in the default case instead of panicking.
- Returning the interface lets callers stay decoupled from whether storage is in-memory or on disk.

## Complexity
`NewServer` is O(k) over k options; `NewStorage` is O(1). Space is O(1) beyond the constructed object (the memory storage's map grows with stored entries).

## Pitfalls
- Apply defaults before applying options, otherwise zero values clobber user choices.
- `MemoryStorage` must initialize its map (done in the factory); writing to a nil map panics.
- Option order matters when two options touch the same field; document precedence.
- The factory must handle the unknown-kind case explicitly and return a non-nil error, and callers must check it before using the returned interface (which is nil on error).

Например: API позволяет 5 запросов/сек — Rate Limiter гарантирует, что клиент не превысит лимит. КАК РАБОТАЕТ (Token Bucket): 1. Есть «ведро» (буферизированный канал) с токенам…

## Summary
Implement a rate limiter using the token-bucket algorithm backed by a `time.Ticker`. `NewRateLimiter(rate, burst)` creates a limiter that allows `burst` immediate requests and then refills one token every `1s/rate`. Callers invoke `Wait()` which blocks until a token is available; `Close()` stops the background refill goroutine.

## Why it matters
Rate limiting protects services from overload and enforces API quotas. The token-bucket pattern (a buffered channel as the bucket plus a ticker as the refiller) is a canonical Go concurrency idiom that appears in clients, gateways, and any throttled I/O path.

## Idea
- A buffered channel `tokens` of capacity `burst` is the bucket; each `struct{}` is a token costing zero bytes.
- The bucket is pre-filled with `burst` tokens so the first `burst` calls pass instantly.
- A background goroutine listens on `ticker.C`; on each tick it tries a non-blocking send (`select` with `default`) so a full bucket simply drops the surplus token.
- `Wait()` receives from `tokens`, blocking when empty — this is the throttle.
- `Close()` closes the `stop` channel; the goroutine sees it, stops the ticker to free resources, and returns.

## Complexity
`Wait()` is O(1) channel receive; refill goroutine does O(1) work per tick. Space is O(burst) for the channel buffer plus one goroutine and one ticker.

## Pitfalls
- Forgetting the non-blocking send (`default`) makes the refill goroutine block on a full bucket, freezing the ticker drain.
- Not calling `ticker.Stop()` on shutdown leaks the ticker's resources.
- `rate = 0` causes a division-by-zero panic in `time.Second / time.Duration(rate)`.
- Closing `stop` more than once panics; `Close()` must be called at most once.

## Summary
Demonstrate Python generators and iterators: an infinite Fibonacci generator, a chunked reader, a generator pipeline (numbers → even-only → squared), a class-based `Countdown` iterator, a recursive `flatten`, and an `accumulator` coroutine driven by `send()`. The output is the values each producer yields when consumed.

## Why it matters
Generators give lazy, memory-efficient streaming and compose into pipelines, which is central to data processing, file streaming, and ETL code. `send()`-based coroutines are the foundation of cooperative concurrency patterns in Python.

## Idea
- A generator function pauses at each `yield` and resumes on the next `next()`, so `fibonacci()` can be infinite yet consumed finitely via `take`-style loops.
- Pipelines chain generators: each stage consumes its upstream lazily, so `squared(even_only(numbers(10)))` processes one element end-to-end at a time.
- A class implements the iterator protocol with `__iter__` returning self and `__next__` raising `StopIteration` when done (`Countdown`).
- `flatten` uses `yield from` to recurse into nested lists, delegating to sub-generators.
- The `accumulator` coroutine must be primed with one `next()` (or `send(None)`) before `send(value)` can inject data; `value = yield total` receives the sent value and returns the running total.

## Complexity
Each generator yields in O(1) amortized per element; `flatten` is O(n) over total elements with recursion depth equal to nesting depth. Space is O(1) per generator (no materialized lists) aside from recursion/result collection.

## Pitfalls
- Calling `send(value)` before priming the coroutine raises `TypeError: can't send non-None value to a just-started generator`.
- Iterating an infinite generator (`fibonacci`, real `Naturals`) without a bound (`take`, `islice`) hangs.
- A class iterator that returns a fresh state from `__iter__` vs `self` changes whether it is single- or multi-pass; here `Countdown` is single-pass.
- `isinstance(item, list)` only flattens `list`; strings or tuples are treated as scalars, which may or may not be intended.
